canonical_statement: The review aimed to summarize existing recommendations and supporting evidence on vitamin K given after birth to prevent haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We looked at existing recommendations and supporting evidence on the effectiveness of vitamin K given after birth in preventing the haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (HDN).

canonical_statement: The abstract reports a literature search through 10 December 2019 using key terms and manual searching of selected sources.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: We conducted a literature search up to the 10th of December 2019 by using key terms and manual search in selected sources.

canonical_statement: The body reports a selected-source search on 10 June 2019 and a PubMed search on 28 June 2019 that returned 121 records; screening yielded two reviews, two cohort studies, and two position papers in addition to previously identified material.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The search was conducted on the 10th of June 2019... The search was conducted on the 28th of June 2019... and returned 121 manuscripts... we included two reviews, two cohort studies, and two position papers.

canonical_statement: The review reports an estimated HDN incidence of 35 per 100,000 live births among infants without vitamin K prophylaxis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Among infants who had not received vitamin K prophylaxis at birth, the incidence of HDN was estimated at 35 (10.5 to 80) per 100,000 live births.

population.label: Newborn infants without vitamin K prophylaxis

concept.text: Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn incidence

canonical_statement: For high-income countries, the review reports an estimated HDN incidence of 8.8 per 100,000 live births among infants without vitamin K prophylaxis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: being lower in high income countries at 8.8 (5.8 to 17.8) per 100,000 live births

population.label: Newborn infants without vitamin K prophylaxis in high-income countries

concept.text: Haemorrhagic disease of the newborn incidence

canonical_statement: The review reports that the Puckett Cochrane review included 13 randomized or quasi-randomized trials, mainly term or uncomplicated infants, with eight trials limited to exclusively breastfed infants and publication dates from 1960 to 1998.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The 13 identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs included only term infants or infants without complications... and eight of them included only infants who were on exclusive breastfeeding. These studies were published between 1960 and 1998.

canonical_statement: The review notes poor methodological quality in the older trials, including undescribed or incorrect randomization and high losses to follow-up.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: authors of the review acknowledge the poor methodological quality of the included trials (randomization not described or incorrect, high losses to follow-up)

canonical_statement: The review reports that WHO graded the evidence supporting vitamin K prophylaxis as moderate to low quality.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the quality of this evidence was graded as moderate to low by the authors of the WHO recommendations

canonical_statement: The review reports that a single intramuscular vitamin K dose reduced clinical bleeding at 1 to 7 days versus placebo or no intervention, RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.96.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: relative risk [RR] 0.73; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.56 to 0.96

population.label: Term or uncomplicated newborn infants in trials summarized by Puckett et al.

canonical_statement: The same comparison was reported with a risk difference of -0.02, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.00, for clinical bleeding at 1 to 7 days.

population.label: Term or uncomplicated newborn infants in trials summarized by Puckett et al.

canonical_statement: The review found no randomized trials directly comparing oral and intramuscular vitamin K prophylaxis in newborns.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: There are no randomized trials comparing the oral and intramuscular (IM) route of vitamin K prophylaxis in newborns.

canonical_statement: From surveillance studies summarized by Sankar et al., the review reports that 1 mg intramuscular or subcutaneous vitamin K reduced late HDN versus placebo, RR 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.10.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: From two studies, 1 mg of IM or subcutaneous vitamin K prophylaxis reduced incidence of late HDN when compared to placebo (RR 0.02; 95%CI 0.00 to 0.10).

canonical_statement: The review states that recent European surveillance data did not show a significant difference between intramuscular and completed oral regimens for preventing late HDN.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the more recent data from surveillance systems does not seem to support a significant difference between the IM and the oral route for preventing late HDN

canonical_statement: The effectiveness of oral vitamin K prophylaxis depends on completing multiple doses; incomplete oral prophylaxis has been identified in newborns who developed HDN.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The efficacy of the oral regimen relies on the compliance with the protocol (multiple doses). Incomplete oral prophylaxis have been detected in newborns with HDN receiving the oral regimen.

canonical_statement: Studies summarized by the review found no significant difference in PIVKA-II between single-dose oral and intramuscular vitamin K at 1 to 7 days, 2 weeks, 1 month, or 3 months.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: There were no significant differences on PIVKA II at several endpoints (1 to 7 days, 2 weeks, 1 month and 3 months)

canonical_statement: The review reports that the 2018 Ardell Cochrane review found no randomized trial of vitamin K by any route versus no vitamin K in preterm infants, and identified one three-arm randomized trial of 80 infants under 32 weeks gestation.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: No RCT looking at vitamin K via any route of administration versus no vitamin K was identified. Only one RCT comparing three arms of prophylactic vitamin K (0.5 mg IM, 0.2 mg IM and 0.2 mg IV) in 80 preterm babies under 32 weeks of gestational age was identified.

canonical_statement: The review reports low certainty for all preterm outcomes because the evidence came from one small trial.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The certainty of the evidence was graded as low for all the outcomes, due to the small sample size from one trial.

canonical_statement: The review describes local hematoma, infection, and neuromuscular injury from properly administered intramuscular vitamin K as very uncommon, while acknowledging injection pain.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the risk of local hematomas, infections and neuromuscular damage at the site of the injection is very low. Although the IM injection is likely to be painful

canonical_statement: The review concludes that all newborns should receive vitamin K prophylaxis and that both oral and intramuscular prophylaxis prevent classical HDN.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: All newborns should receive vitamin K prophylaxis, as it has been proven that oral and intramuscular prophylactic vitamin K given after birth is effective for preventing classical HDN.

canonical_statement: The review states that no randomized trials tested vitamin K prophylaxis for prevention of late HDN.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: There are no randomized trials looking at the efficacy of vitamin K supplement on late HDN.

canonical_statement: The review concludes that completed oral and intramuscular regimens appear similarly effective for classical and late HDN in European surveillance data, while recognizing the lack of direct randomized comparison.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: it seems that there is no significant difference between the IM and the oral regimens for preventing classical and late HDN, provided that the oral regimen is duly completed.

canonical_statement: The review states that oral vitamin K is not appropriate for newborns with biliary atresia.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The oral route is not appropriate for newborns with biliary atresia.

canonical_statement: The review concludes that evidence for vitamin K prophylaxis in preterm infants is scarce.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Evidence assessing vitamin K prophylaxis in preterm infants is scarce.

canonical_statement: The review reports that WHO recommends 1 mg intramuscular vitamin K for all newborns after birth, with a strong recommendation and moderate-quality evidence.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: All newborns should be given 1 mg of vitamin K intramuscularly (IM) after birth

canonical_statement: The review reports that NICE recommends a single 1 mg intramuscular vitamin K dose and offers oral vitamin K as a second-line option when parents decline intramuscular administration, with multiple oral doses required.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Vitamin K should be administered as a single dose of 1 mg intramuscularly... If parents decline intramuscular vitamin K... oral vitamin K should be offered as a second-line option.

canonical_statement: The review reports that the AAP policy then cited recommended 0.5 to 1 mg vitamin K1 intramuscularly as a single dose for all newborns.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Vitamin K1 should be given to all newborns as a single, intramuscular dose of 0.5 to 1 mg.

canonical_statement: The review reports that ESPGHAN listed 1 mg intramuscular vitamin K at birth or specified multidose oral regimens for healthy newborns and considered the oral route inappropriate for preterm, unwell, cholestatic, malabsorptive, or otherwise high-risk newborns.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Healthy newborn infants should either receive: (a) 1 mg of Vitamin K1 by IM injection at birth... The oral route is not appropriate for preterm infants and for newborns who are unwell, have cholestasis or impaired intestinal absorption

canonical_statement: The review reports that CADTH recommended intramuscular vitamin K within 6 hours of birth, 0.5 mg for birthweight 1500 g or less and 1 mg for birthweight 1500 g or more, with a multidose oral option if intramuscular prophylaxis is refused.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Single intramuscular dose of vitamin K (0.5 mg for birthweight ≤1500 g or 1.0 mg for birthweight ≥1500 g) should be administered to all newborns within the first 6 h after birth.
